facts: President Trump held a White House press conference on a Friday after a three-day trip to Asia, during which he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the first-ever three-way meeting of the three leaders.

Trump announced that he and Xi agreed to establish 'joint guardrails' on artificial intelligence, which he also referred to as 'super intelligence,' but provided no details on timing, scope, or enforcement.
Trump said the U.S. will not allow American companies to build AI data centers outside the United States and indicated companies that do so would face penalties.

Trump's nominee to lead CISA, Michael LoSapio, had a Senate confirmation hearing the day before the press conference in which he declined to say who won the 2020 presidential election and said he did not consider the January 6, 2021 Capitol events an attack.

During the trip, Trump signed a trade agreement with Thailand described as a 'substantial conclusion' with details still to be finalized, and the Xi-Putin meeting produced only an agreement to continue discussing nuclear risk reduction.

ladder.analysis: The press conference followed a high-profile Asia trip framed by the administration as a diplomatic triumph, but the concrete outcomes were limited: a preliminary trade deal with Thailand, a pledge to keep talking about nuclear risk with Russia and China, and an unspecified AI 'guardrails' agreement with Beijing. The announcement is notable because it marks a shift from Trump's prior resistance to AI regulation, though the lack of detail leaves its actual impact unclear. Simultaneously, the administration is navigating internal tension over China chip exports—Commerce Secretary Lutnick has favored sales while Treasury Secretary Bessent has taken a more hawkish stance—compounded by scrutiny of chip sales to Chinese firms with reported military ties. The cybersecurity leadership change and the stalled CISA nomination are significant because that agency oversees election security, raising questions about preparedness ahead of the 2028 election cycle.
ladder.steelman: Across the specifics—AI guardrails without detail, a trade pact still being finalized, a cybersecurity post filled by a policy (not operational) appointee, and an unresolved chip-export policy—the throughline is a gap between the administration's framing of decisive wins and the preliminary, unresolved nature of the actual agreements and appointments.
ladder.implications: Key unresolved threads—the scope of any U.S.-China AI guardrails, the administration's final posture on chip exports to China, the fate of the CISA directorship amid the LoSapio nomination, and the as-yet-unfinished Thailand trade deal—will likely shape near-term policy fights and may bear directly on election security infrastructure heading toward 2028.

ladder.analysis: Jeffries' ascension to speaker would mark a historic first, arriving amid a broader generational and demographic shift in the incoming Congress. The transition unfolds through a well-established but intricate process: the outgoing Republican-controlled Congress continues governing during a lame-duck period, working against a mid-December funding deadline, while newly elected members undergo orientation and parties select their leadership for the new term. Because Democrats will control both chambers starting in January, they will gain committee chairmanships with subpoena power, enabling investigations into the Trump administration, even as Trump retains veto power that would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override — meaning unified Democratic control does not guarantee policy outcomes without some negotiation with the White House.
ladder.steelman: Regardless of the historic nature of Jeffries' rise, the mechanics of the transition — a funding deadline, a contested Senate Democratic leadership race, and the procedural handoff between a lame-duck Congress and the incoming one — will shape what either party can actually accomplish once the new Congress convenes.
ladder.implications: The coming weeks will test whether outgoing lawmakers can resolve the December 11 funding deadline before Congress adjourns, while the outcome of the Senate Democratic leadership race could influence how an incoming Democrat-controlled Congress approaches negotiations with the Trump White House on spending, the debt ceiling, and oversight once the 120th Congress convenes in January.

ladder.analysis: The story sits at the intersection of AI industrial policy and U.S.-China tech competition. Trump's threatened ban on offshore AI data centers follows a week of escalating chip-export controls aimed at preventing advanced U.S. semiconductors from reaching China, and comes as major tech 'hyperscalers' like Meta, Google and Anthropic have been building or leasing data-center capacity in Canada and Europe partly in response to domestic pushback over energy use, noise and land clearance. Enforcement mechanics of Trump's proposed ban remain undefined, and he presented it as a fresh idea even to his own administration, underscoring its preliminary, non-policy status.

Trump argues domestic communities should capitalize on data centers rather than block them, saying localities should "make them pay you... take advantage, don't shut them off."

ladder.steelman: Both the chip-smuggling warnings from a Republican senator and the data-center ban threat from the Republican president reflect the same underlying anxiety—that U.S. AI infrastructure and technology could end up strengthening China—even as the administration has yet to detail how either the export licensing or the proposed overseas data-center ban would actually be enforced.
ladder.implications: Whether Trump's threatened ban becomes formal policy will depend on administration follow-through and legal mechanisms for restricting private companies' overseas investments, while the chip-licensing regime and Cotton's criticism of Lutnick suggest continued scrutiny—both from allies and critics—over how tightly the administration controls AI chip exports to China.

stories.headline: Ukraine war: Zelensky defends Crimea Bridge strikes as 'fair response'; Russian cargo ship hit in Gulf of Finland
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling them a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine. In an interview with the BBC, Zelensky rejected Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim that the bridge is "exclusively civilian" in use, pointing to online images of tanks and military hardware using the route as a supply line. "If Putin used the internet, he could see that," Zelensky said. This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it and one of its support arches into the sea, rendering it unusable for road traffic. Ukraine's General Staff declared that "the short supply route from Russian territory has been destroyed," while the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said the operation "shook the myth of Russia's greatness." According to Al Jazeera, it was Ukraine's fourth and most complex operation on the bridge, possibly crippling its rail section as well. Bloomberg reported that cleanup of the downed bridge will take Russia months, according to Ukraine.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight, killing a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old female medic in Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials said the boy was in a playground at the time. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet-powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city. Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne in the north-west. Zelensky described Putin as a "killer," in response to US President Donald Trump referring to Putin this week as his "friend."

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was there to show that Europe was united in its support. "The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said. He called Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing an "outrageous provocation," adding that the timing seemed "more than a coincidence." Asked about NATO's response, Streeting said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin, whom he called a "cold-blooded killer." Streeting's visit came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe has "a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic." US envoy Jared Kushner said President Trump wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side." Putin has so far rejected any European role in US-led peace talks but earlier this week invited European representatives to Moscow. The Berlin meeting came hours after Putin held trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, in an international maritime area. The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving further details. It added that temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland were reinstated for safety reasons. Russia has not publicly commented on the incident.

stories.headline: Russian strike kills two, wounds 60 in Zelenskyy's hometown Kryvyi Rih
body: A Russian ballistic missile strike on the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded at least 60 others on Friday evening, local officials said Saturday. The dead included a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while six children were among the wounded. Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the city administration, reported that about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools, and an industrial facility were damaged. He added that Russian forces launched further missiles after emergency workers arrived, striking rescuers, medical personnel, and utility crews. Footage from Ukraine's emergency services appeared to show additional strikes during the rescue operation.

The attack followed Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a 'painful' response to Ukraine's strikes this week on the Kerch Bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia, a vital supply route for Russian forces. Moscow confirmed a further strike on Kryvyi Rih on Friday night, saying a thermal power plant was hit along with a power substation in the Rivne region, both of which it claimed supply electricity to Ukraine's military industry.

The violence came as two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in southeastern Poland, a NATO member, on Friday. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident as a 'deliberate provocation' and questioned its timing alongside military exercises involving European countries. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the airspace violation on Saturday and pledged that the alliance would defend Polish territory.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, Russian attacks killed two people in the southern Zaporizhia region, struck a cargo vessel near Odesa, wounded 11 people including two children in Kharkiv, and wounded one person in Kyiv. In Russia, local officials said Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions. Finland reported a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday morning, with Prime Minister Petteri Orpo warning that the war is 'spilling over into our immediate vicinity.'

Russian authorities also reported six deaths, including a child, from a Ukrainian attack on a residential area in Russian-controlled Luhansk in eastern Ukraine. On the diplomatic front, U.S. President Donald Trump said after talks with Putin in China that the Russian leader wanted to end the war diplomatically. Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv on Saturday he remained less convinced that Putin was prepared to compromise, noting Moscow's demand for Ukrainian withdrawal from the entire Donbas region, which Kyiv refuses. Zelenskyy reaffirmed Ukraine's ambition to join NATO, while Washington has discussed offering security guarantees resembling the alliance's collective-defense commitments.

stories.headline: COP31 Climate Talks in Deadlock as Overtime Exceeds 24 Hours; Fossil Fuels and Finance Remain Sticking Points
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on AP
body: Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, are in deadlock after running more than 24 hours into overtime, with countries unable to agree on a new global climate deal. The main sticking points are the absence of any reference to reducing the world’s demand for fossil fuels in the draft agreement, and a push from the Africa Group for commitments to increase adaptation finance—which the European Union has previously said it would not support.

A group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft that excluded fossil fuel language, which was removed after pressure from fossil-fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia. “It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it,” said Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro. France’s Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, criticized references to carbon capture technology as a license to keep burning oil and gas, saying, “We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening.” Meanwhile, Ghana’s environment minister and chair of the African Group, Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, said, “We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries.”

For the first time at a COP, the agreement—known as the Antalya Accords—could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5°C has been missed, entering a period scientists call “overshoot.” Outside the talks, renewable energy is growing rapidly: solar panels contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth this year, outstripping oil and gas. However, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed in Shenzhen to increase oil production amid fuel supply disruption from the Iran War.

Australia’s climate minister Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, argued that the summit should focus on implementation and the move toward clean energy. China, the largest greenhouse gas emitter, endorsed a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035, but a senior Chinese adviser, Wang Yi, said meeting that target would be harder if the electricity must come entirely from low-carbon sources. The second draft text downgraded the electrification pledge to a voluntary option. China also voiced concern about trade barriers such as US tariffs and the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, with Wang calling for unified approaches on trade at future COPs.

Climate activists and environmental groups have slammed the negotiations. “I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa. Observers noted that Turkey’s lead negotiator walked out of crucial talks, leaving many countries feeling “disrespected.” Negotiators who were due to fly out Sunday are now moving flights to Monday, but not all countries have the funding or capacity to extend their stay. If the summit loses the critical number of nations needed to pass an agreement, it could end with no deal and be suspended—a step taken only once since COP meetings began in 1995.

stories.headline: Denmark Accuses Russia of Plotting to Kill US-Ukrainian Rapper, Expels Diplomat
body: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American rapper on Danish soil and has expelled Russia’s defense attaché in response, Danish authorities said Friday. The target, identified by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner—whose real name is Albert Vasiliev and who holds U.S. and Ukrainian nationality—was set to perform at a concert north of Copenhagen on September 25 when police arrested three men traveling in a vehicle near the venue. Firearms and knives were found in the car, and two of the individuals have since been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service; both pleaded not guilty, according to local media.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen announced the expulsion of Russia’s defense attaché, who must leave the country within seven days, after summoning the Russian ambassador. “We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” Rasmussen told a news conference. He described the alleged plot as Russian “intimidation” and an attempt to make Denmark “waver” in its support for Ukraine. The head of Denmark’s security and intelligence service (PET), Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, said, “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian intelligence services.” PET stated that the individuals allegedly involved were associated with the outlawed Danish gang Loyal to Familia, “known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity.” Police stopped the vehicle at about 9:55 p.m.—five minutes before the concert was due to begin—and one suspect had purchased a ticket to the show, according to court documents.

The incident comes after Russia’s FSB security service in July accused Vasiliev and Ukrainian authorities of organizing a “terrorist attack” on military facilities in Russia, an allegation the rapper denied on social media. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the plot “is a clear illustration of the grave security situation Denmark and Europe find ourselves in. We are facing a Russia under pressure which is acting more aggressively and is more willing to take risks.” The European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned what she called “the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainan citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services,” adding, “This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable.” European Council President António Costa said, “We will not be intimidated. Russia’s tactics and threats will not weaken the European Union’s resolve to continue supporting Ukraine.”

Russia’s embassy in Copenhagen called the accusations “unsubstantiated” and said Denmark failed to provide evidence of Moscow’s involvement. In a statement, the embassy claimed a “Danish model” had emerged, which it described as a “Russian trace” allegedly being discovered and “exploited for a propaganda spectacle,” accusing Denmark of “provocations” intended to “frighten the Danish population in order to justify … a prolonged confrontation with Russia.” Russian state media cited the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it would respond to the expulsion “accordingly.”

Rasmussen also said Denmark is pushing for the European Union to restrict Russian travel within the Schengen zone. In a message to senior European diplomats, he proposed that the EU halt tourist visas for Russians, cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports across the Schengen area, and issue more limited visas that do not allow travel to other Schengen countries. “We must take concrete actions that project European strength and decisiveness,” his message said. Von der Leyen said the EU would soon propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence. The alleged plot, which PET chief Kieffer-Kristensen described as unprecedented in Denmark, has heightened concerns about Russian hybrid threats as the war in Ukraine continues.

stories.headline: Anthropic's record IPO fails to stem market sell-off as 'smart money' shifts
body: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering, which raised $81 billion after pricing above its expected range at $83 per share, failed to halt a broader market sell-off on Friday as new data shows U.S. corporations have shifted from buying back shares to issuing them, adding supply that the four-year-old bull market must absorb.

According to a recent analysis by Acadian Asset Management, net new issuance of shares equaled 3.1% of total market capitalization as of late last week. Portfolio manager Owen Lamont wrote in a letter to investors this month that 'no matter how you measure it, U.S. corporations have changed their behavior over the past two years, switching from repurchasing in 2024 to issuing today.' He added: 'The question you should be asking is: Why is the smart money selling?'

The shift marks a reversal from the era of net repurchases, which had helped boost share prices by shrinking the number of shares available for trading and increasing earnings per share. Now, increased equity supply is acting as a potential headwind. The Baker-Wurgler equity share, which measures equity issuance as a share of total stock and bond issuance, peaked at about 18% in 2021 and has risen in recent months but remains below that peak, Lamont noted.

Recent large equity deals include Oracle's filing to sell $20 billion in stock through an at-the-market program and a separate $10 billion common-share issuance in November; Meta's $25 billion common-stock offering and $12.5 billion in mandatory convertible preferred shares in October; Alphabet's $84.8 billion equity raise in June to fund AI infrastructure; and SpaceX's $85.7 billion IPO in June after underwriters exercised their overallotment. Federal Reserve data show debt gross issuance rose first in 2020, followed by equity issuance in 2021; more recently, debt issuance began climbing in 2024, followed by a surge in equity issuance in 2026.

Lamont wrote that 'before 2026, firms were net repurchasers of equity, consistent with the idea that they viewed their shares as undervalued. Today, for whatever reason, firms are issuing equity on net.' He said he cannot rule out that the market is in an AI bubble now. Anthropic's stock, which debuted this week, was falling on Friday and dragging the broader market with it, underscoring investor unease despite the strong initial demand for the frontier AI laboratory's shares.

stories.headline: FDA rejects Capricor's Duchenne muscular dystrophy therapy over data integrity concerns
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Friday declined to approve Capricor Therapeutics' experimental cell therapy deramiocel for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, citing serious data integrity problems in a key clinical trial that undermined the reliability of the evidence. The agency issued a Complete Response Letter, determining that the available data did not meet the required standard for approval. Shares of Capricor plunged 72% in extended trading following the announcement.

Deramiocel was intended to preserve upper-limb function in patients with Duchenne, a fatal genetic disease that causes progressive muscle weakness, loss of mobility, heart complications and premature death. The FDA's decision follows a lengthy review that included two randomized clinical trials, both of which failed to show that deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in the arms. In July, an FDA advisory committee voted 9–3 that the evidence did not establish deramiocel's effectiveness for Duchenne-related heart disease, prompting Capricor to amend its application to focus on upper-limb function using additional 24-month open-label extension data from the Phase 3 HOPE-3 trial. The agency treated that amendment as a major change and moved the decision deadline to November 22.

The FDA identified deficiencies in the conduct of the HOPE-3 study that compromised the reliability of the trial data, according to a statement from the Muscular Dystrophy Association. Capricor has disputed the FDA's assessment of its clinical evidence and is evaluating its next steps. The company's CEO, Linda Marbán, had said earlier in November that the application was in its final review stages and that Capricor was advancing launch preparations while pacing spending to the regulatory timeline. The company is also pursuing independent commercialization amid an ongoing arbitration with Nippon Shinyaku's unit NS Pharma over a prior distribution agreement.

The Muscular Dystrophy Association issued a statement on Saturday expressing disappointment, calling the decision a heavy blow for the Duchenne community. 'We know this decision is a heavy blow for the Duchenne community, and our hearts are with the families who have waited, hoped, and fought for a new treatment,' the organization said. 'We are grateful to the FDA for its thorough review and to Capricor for its continued fight to bring a treatment to this community.' The MDA added that it seeks to learn more about the data integrity issues and will work with Capricor and advocates to understand next steps. The organization reaffirmed its commitment to accelerating research and advocating for regulatory processes that balance urgency with safety and effectiveness standards.

This is the second rejection for deramiocel; the FDA previously issued a Complete Response Letter in July 2025 after the initial application seeking approval for cardiomyopathy associated with Duchenne was found to lack substantial evidence of effectiveness. Patients with Duchenne, primarily boys, have few treatment options, especially those who have already lost the ability to walk. Capricor has said management does not expect the arbitration with NS Pharma to delay patient access if deramiocel is ever approved, but for now the therapy remains investigational and not FDA-approved.

stories.headline: James Webb telescope reveals aftermath of star swallowing another star in Andromeda
body: Astronomers have captured the first direct evidence of a stellar merger in progress, witnessing a smaller star spiral into a giant supergiant in the Andromeda galaxy. Using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope along with decades of ground- and space-based observations, researchers reconstructed the event in which a companion star about 70% as massive as the Sun plunged into a supergiant seven times the Sun’s mass, 350 times its radius, and 18,000 times its brightness. The merger, nicknamed Bao and officially designated AT 2025abao, was observed by Webb just 47 days after the eruption peaked, the earliest follow-up of such an event. The findings were published in Nature.

The two stars had existed as a binary system for thousands of years before the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion. Once that interaction started, the merger took only seven additional orbits—about seven years—far faster than previously observed mergers between smaller stars. 'We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years,' said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona. 'One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!' The outburst was detected on October 17, 2025, by the Zwicky Transient Facility. Webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgent Director’s Discretionary Time program.

The process is known as common envelope evolution. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer layers, resistance slowed its orbit and drained orbital energy, causing the companion to spiral deeper into the giant’s core. The final encounter was 'almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star,' said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University. Webb’s mid-infrared measurements revealed dust expelled by the giant star over hundreds of years, helping scientists confirm the merger had occurred. Simulations led by co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University, showed that the smaller star, nicknamed 'Little Bao,' was dragged deep into the core of 'Big Bao,' releasing immense energy.

Warning signs appeared years earlier. In February 2023, astronomers examining archived data from NASA’s retired NEOWISE mission noticed unusual brightness variations. By September 2024, the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) detected increasing brightness and dust release. In July 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx telescope observed Bao rapidly fading in visible light while brightening in infrared. The systematic monitoring allowed scientists to publish a study just before the eruption. 'Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,' said first author Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia. 'Webb’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger.'

The discovery is significant because it provides real-time measurements of how efficiently common envelope evolution transfers energy and expels material. Such systems can eventually produce neutron stars, black holes, gravitational waves, or millisecond pulsars. The research received partial funding from NASA’s Astrophysics Data Analysis Program. With NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope preparing extensive surveys, scientists expect many more such events. 'There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead,' Karambelkar said. The merged star, Bao, now contains the legacy of both original stars, and future observations will determine how its mass settles as it evolves.

stories.headline: California AG subpoenas Nvidia; questions mount over Huang's management style
body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening announced that the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following revelations about former CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy. The investigation seeks to determine whether Nvidia's advanced GPUs or confidential information were shared with China, and whether the company misled investors and the public about the risks. 'The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,' Bonta said in a statement.

The subpoena comes after a turbulent period for the chipmaker. Huang resigned last week following additional disclosures of extramarital affairs with Nvidia employees. Thousands of employees have signed a letter requesting his return, but the company's board—now chaired by Harvey Jones—has stated it has no intention of reinstating him. The board has hired an outside law firm and an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is probing the ties between Alice Huang (not related to Jensen) and the Chinese government.

Separately, reporting in The New York Times has detailed a management style at Nvidia reportedly built on fear. According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that because Nvidia's wealth made it impossible to motivate employees with money, humiliation was the only remaining lever. The newspaper cited instances where Huang told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would 'rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.' In 2005, former HR chief Michael Winston threatened to sue and called Huang's conduct the most abusive he had seen; Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. A spokesman for Huang has dismissed the allegations as fabrications.

The broader regulatory and congressional scrutiny is intensifying. The U.S. Congress is preparing to subpoena Huang over the affair, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly launching a civil probe into whether Nvidia's public disclosures misled investors. Democratic representatives have opened an inquiry into the Trump administration's handling of Nvidia's chip sales to China, with a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asking the department to preserve records about an arrangement they called 'questionable and illegal.' Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him. 'Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,' Bonta wrote.

stories.headline: YouTube reportedly preparing $3 billion settlement over social media addiction claims
body: YouTube is reportedly preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of U.S. school districts to settle claims that its platform's "addictive design" harmed children, according to Bloomberg. The agreement, which sources say has been reached "in principle," would also require YouTube to introduce new safeguards for teens, the report states.

The potential settlement would allow Google, YouTube's parent company, to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by school districts accusing YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first "bellwether" trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was scheduled to begin in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court. The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California, judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants.
Google did not immediately respond to The Verge's request for comment.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. That agreement also included stricter safeguards for teens, but Meta is pushing TikTok and YouTube to implement similar measures. As part of the deal, Meta will only pay the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out comparable changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.

stories.headline: China-Linked Hackers' AI Agents Exploited Medical Software Zero-Day, Amazon Says
body: Amazon's threat intelligence team detected in September a 48-hour campaign in which autonomous AI agents operated by a China-linked threat actor exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open-source tool for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The agents targeted IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.

The activity was spotted when Amazon found an exposed, unauthenticated instance of Cairn, an open-source AI penetration testing framework, which revealed the operator's prompts and the agents' output. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and instructed them to obtain shell access. After identifying MONAI Label on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. 'In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,' Amazon reported.

In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs at interpreter startup, ultimately achieving a root shell. The operator then provided a proxy that tunneled into a second university and directed the agents to target other devices on its network. Amazon noted that the server the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, inferring the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel.

Amazon assessed with high confidence that the flaw was a zero-day, citing 'the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.' MONAI Label's developers published an advisory this week rating the bug critical, affecting versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, allowing anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon attributed the attack with moderate confidence to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor, based on the language used in prompts, the time zone in scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. The company did not name a specific group.

stories.headline: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Solve Riemann Hypothesis With Help From Claude; Human Mathematician Also Releases Proof
body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by Anthropic, announced on Friday that he has produced a formal proof of the Riemann hypothesis using a non-public version of the company's Claude chatbot, according to reports from TechCrunch, The New York Times, and BBC. The proof, written in the Lean programming language, spans over 250,000 pages. Alpöge said he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday to ask how to announce the finding, adding that "the precise timing is horrible" because it came a day after Anthropic's public stock market debut. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier," he wrote in an essay, describing his obsession with the problem since childhood and saying he "could not live" if he waited longer to release the result.

The Riemann hypothesis, dating to 1859, is one of the Millennium Prize problems and posits that prime numbers follow a hidden structure along the number line. A correct proof would be among the most significant in mathematics. Alpöge described the experience of working with Claude as a "stream-of-consciousness jaunt" in which the model "flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Several mathematicians on the Zulip chat platform, including MIT's Andrew Sutherland, said they have independently confirmed that Alpöge's Lean code compiles successfully. However, prominent mathematician Terence Tao noted that verification of the proof itself is still some way off, though he added that "in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task."

Separately, Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo released a human-written proof of the General Riemann hypothesis, the result of 12 years of work. Stanford professor Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematics Association, posted the proof, writing that "it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft." Masullo wrote in his introduction: "If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere." Neither proof has yet been fully verified by the broader mathematical community.

Alpöge also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, co-authored with NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster. The announcement follows a series of AI-driven mathematical breakthroughs this year. In September, OpenAI claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools solved part of a Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours, using more than 10,000 AI agents. That proof has not been confirmed, and a group of mathematics scholars criticized such announcements as "detrimental to the science of mathematics," warning of "a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose." OpenAI later released claims of solutions or progress on 372 more outstanding problems, which will take months or longer to verify.

Alpöge has committed to producing a human-intelligible explanation of his Riemann hypothesis proof. For now, the mathematics community is working through the Lean-formalized result. As one number theorist, Chris Birkbeck of the University of East Anglia, posted on Zulip, the cohomology bound in the proof "genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel's purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more." The post received 20 reactions with the 🤯 emoji.
